answers.primary: A subagent: define a test-runner agent (an agent definition file under .claude/agents/) that executes the suite in its own context window and is instructed to return only the failing test names, their assertions and error messages. The parent conversation receives just that final report, never the raw log stream.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill (or plain slash command) holding the same run-and-filter procedure, rejected because a skill executes inline in the invoking conversation, so every line of suite output lands in the main transcript before any filtering can happen.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split: the harness owns the boundary (the subagent's transcript is discarded and only its final message is handed back), while the model owns the quality of the filtering, since nothing verifies that every failure made it into the summary.
answers.context_boundary: The work runs in a fresh subagent context. Crossing in: only the invocation prompt the parent composes. Crossing out: only the subagent's final text message. The thousands of log lines live and die inside the subagent's window.
answers.lifecycle: Runs when the parent delegates to the agent, either by explicit name or by description match, and stops when the subagent emits its final message. Nothing persists to the next invocation; each run starts empty.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory on content and lossy: the subagent may paraphrase a stack trace, drop a failure, or truncate, and once it returns, the raw output is unrecoverable, so the parent cannot ask a follow-up about a detail that was summarized away. It fails open in that a bad summary still looks like a clean answer.
answers.version_caveat: Custom agent definitions with name/description/tools frontmatter are a stable Claude Code feature and no paid-plan gate applies, but I cannot state from model knowledge alone which release introduced the model: and tools: frontmatter keys, so the exact minimum version should be checked against the installed build.

answers.primary: A subagent whose definition carries an explicit tools allowlist limited to the read-only tools (Read, Grep, Glob) with Write, Edit, NotebookEdit and Bash omitted entirely. Because the harness builds the subagent's tool schema from that list, the mutation tools are simply not present for it to call.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook that denies Write/Edit/Bash for the reviewer, rejected because it leaves the capability visible and merely intercepts each attempt, so the guarantee depends on the hook enumerating every mutation path rather than on the capability being absent.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Tool availability is decided when the subagent is constructed, so neither the agent's own instructions nor a mid-task decision by the model can re-grant a tool that was never handed to it.
answers.context_boundary: The review runs in the subagent's own context window; the review request crosses in, the review report crosses out, and the file contents it reads stay inside its window and are discarded with it.
answers.lifecycle: Applies for the whole life of every invocation of that agent, from spawn to final report. The allowlist is read when the agent definition is loaded, so edits to the frontmatter take effect on the next load rather than mid-run.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed on writes, which is the point, but over-restriction bites in practice: a reviewer that cannot run git diff, a linter or a type checker tempts you to add Bash back, and Bash silently restores full write capability. Read-only is also not the same as safe, since the agent can still read secrets and surface them in its report.
answers.version_caveat: The dangerous default is omission: a subagent with no tools key inherits the full tool set, so the restriction only exists if the key is present. I also cannot confirm from model knowledge whether MCP-provided tools must be listed individually to be excluded, so that should be verified on the installed version.

answers.primary: This is not an extension mechanism at all; it needs a harness-level ephemeral fork of the current conversation, where the question is answered from a copy of the existing context and neither the question nor the answer is committed to the ongoing transcript. I am not confident of the exact name, keybinding or availability of that affordance in the current build, so I will not invent one.
answers.rejected_alternative: A subagent, rejected because a subagent starts from an empty context and inherits none of the session history, so the parent would have to re-serialize the entire walkthrough into the prompt, which defeats both the "draws on everything discussed" and the "costs no room" requirements.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness, since only the harness decides what is appended to the conversation history; the model cannot un-write its own turn once it has been recorded.
answers.context_boundary: The exchange runs against a copy of the current session context, so the full prior discussion is visible to it, but nothing produced in it crosses back into the persisted transcript.
answers.lifecycle: Triggered by the single aside question, ends when it is answered, and leaves no residue; the next real turn continues from the context as it stood before the question.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open if the affordance is unavailable or invoked incorrectly: the question and its answer are simply appended to the session and permanently consume the context they were meant to avoid. The reverse cost is that any insight from the aside is unavailable later, so a decision made there is invisible to the rest of the session.
answers.version_caveat: No plan or flag gate that I can state with confidence. Because I cannot name the feature or its version from model knowledge alone, the practical caveat is to confirm the current build actually offers a discardable in-context aside before designing a workflow around it; if it does not, no extension mechanism reproduces parent-context inheritance.

answers.primary: A subagent for the regression-test drafting, invoked with a handoff brief that the main agent composes: the characterized bug, the confirmed findings, the ruled-out hypotheses, the config quirks and the relevant stack traces written out verbatim in the invocation prompt. The user re-explains nothing; the parent, which holds the two hours of context, does the serialization.
answers.rejected_alternative: An agent team, rejected as disproportionate here: there is one helper and one deliverable, no peer-to-peer disagreement to resolve, so the coordination machinery of a team buys nothing over a single delegated worker.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. Nothing in the harness copies findings across the boundary, so the completeness of the brief is entirely a model judgement, and the harness only guarantees that whatever is not written into the prompt does not arrive.
answers.context_boundary: The helper runs in a fresh context window. Only the authored brief crosses in, only the drafted tests and a short report cross out; the parent's debugging transcript itself never crosses.
answers.lifecycle: Starts at the moment of delegation and ends when the subagent returns its tests. It does not persist, so a second round of test drafting needs a second brief, and any refinement discovered later has to be re-communicated.
answers.failure_mode: The brief is the single point of failure: a hypothesis the parent forgot to mark as ruled out gets re-explored, and the helper writes tests against a misremembered detail. Also, a Task-style subagent occupies the parent's turn while it runs, so the "keep working on the fix meanwhile" part is not really satisfied unless the build offers a background or teammate variant that runs concurrently, and I cannot confirm that from model knowledge alone.
answers.version_caveat: No paid-plan gate applies to ordinary subagent delegation. The genuinely version-sensitive part is concurrency: whether delegated work can run in the background while the user continues talking to the main agent has changed across releases, so that capability should be checked on the installed version rather than assumed.

answers.primary: A subagent whose definition body is the written procedure and whose tools allowlist is read-only (Read, Grep, Glob, plus whatever read-only retrieval the procedure genuinely needs). The team invokes it by agent name, optionally fronted by a slash command that does nothing but dispatch to it.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill, rejected because a skill's instructions load into the invoking conversation and its steps execute there, so every intermediate file read and command output lands in the caller's transcript, and a skill carries no capability restriction of its own.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness for both properties that matter here: context isolation and the read-only tool set are applied when the subagent is constructed. The model still owns whether it actually follows the procedure's steps in order.
answers.context_boundary: Runs in its own window; the PR reference and any parameters cross in, the finished summary crosses out. Intermediate diffs, file reads and command output are discarded when the subagent ends.
answers.lifecycle: Fires on named invocation, ends at the final summary, and holds no state between runs. Edits to the procedure take effect when the agent definition is next loaded, not mid-run.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed on anything that would write, and fails open on procedure adherence: a long multi-step procedure can be partially skipped and, because the intermediate transcript is thrown away, the skip is unauditable after the fact. The reviewer sees a plausible summary with no way to check which steps actually ran.
answers.version_caveat: The read-only property depends entirely on the tools allowlist being present, since omitting it inherits the full tool set including Bash. I cannot state the minimum version for agent-definition frontmatter from model knowledge alone, and if the procedure needs network retrieval, whether a read-only fetch tool is available may itself be configuration dependent.

answers.primary: Embed the full API-conventions text verbatim in the subagent's own definition file, so it forms part of that agent's system prompt on every spawn. Presence then costs nothing to the model's discretion: the conventions are already in the window before the first token of the task.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill containing the conventions that the worker is told to invoke, rejected because skill loading is progressive and model-discretionary; that makes the guidance discoverable rather than guaranteed, which is exactly the failure already being observed.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split, and the split is the whole point: the harness guarantees the text is present, the model still owns compliance with it. Guaranteed presence is not guaranteed obedience.
answers.context_boundary: The conventions live in the subagent's context from spawn. The parent's loaded copy does not cross the boundary; only the task prompt goes in and the implementation report comes out.
answers.lifecycle: Applies on every invocation of that agent, for the whole run, and stops when the run ends. A change to the conventions requires editing the agent definition and reloading it, typically at the next session or agent load.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory at the compliance layer: the worker can read the conventions and still deviate, and nothing checks the output against them, so a verification hook or reviewer is still needed if conformance must be guaranteed. The duplicated text also drifts from the canonical guide, and if it is long it both taxes every invocation and risks being diluted in the middle of the prompt.
answers.version_caveat: No plan or flag gate applies. The relevant caveat is that whether a subagent automatically inherits project-level memory such as CLAUDE.md has varied across releases and I cannot state the current behaviour with confidence, which is precisely why inheritance should not be relied on and the text should be inlined.

answers.primary: A PreToolUse hook matched to the Bash tool that parses the proposed command, detects mutating SQL (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, TRUNCATE, DROP, ALTER, CREATE, GRANT) and returns a deny decision so the command never executes. Best paired with a positive allowlist of accepted query shapes rather than a blocklist of forbidden ones.
answers.rejected_alternative: A deny rule in the settings permissions list, rejected because those rules match command patterns rather than parse the SQL payload, so they are too coarse to distinguish a SELECT from an UPDATE buried in the arguments of the same database CLI invocation.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook is an external process whose decision the model cannot see around, argue with, or re-run, and it fires for delegated subagent tool calls as well as the main session's.
answers.context_boundary: The hook runs outside every model context, in its own OS process, receiving the tool input as JSON on stdin. Only the deny verdict and its reason string cross back into the worker's context; the worker never gets to attempt the statement.
answers.lifecycle: Fires on every Bash tool call for as long as the hook is configured in settings, from session start onward. Hook configuration is read when the session starts, so adding or editing the hook generally requires a restart to take effect.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed only for what it recognizes, and fails open around the edges: a statement in a .sql file passed by path, a heredoc, an encoded or aliased command, a chained pipeline, a different client binary, or an MCP database tool that never routes through Bash all evade string inspection. An over-eager pattern also fails the other way, blocking a legitimate SELECT whose column name happens to contain "update".
answers.version_caveat: Hook deny semantics have two forms, the exit-code convention and a structured JSON permission decision, and I cannot state from model knowledge alone which release introduced the structured form or how a hook crash or timeout is treated, so both should be verified on the installed version. The durable fix regardless of version is a read-only database credential, which no Claude Code version can undo.

answers.primary: A dynamic workflow launched by name that runs the cleanup in the session with a tool set that excludes the user-question tool, so the routine has no channel to interrupt with and the restriction lapses on its own at the user's next message. I am describing the intended shape rather than a file format I can confirm, since I cannot state the workflow definition syntax from model knowledge alone.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook that denies the question tool, rejected on lifecycle rather than on enforcement: a hook is session-wide and has no notion of "until the user speaks again", so restoring the capability would require the routine to toggle state on disk, which is exactly the manual re-enable the requirement rules out.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness, which decides what tools are in the turn's schema; the model cannot re-grant itself an interruption channel that the harness withheld.
answers.context_boundary: Runs inside the invoking session's context, which is what lets it use the user's working state, and everything it does is recorded in the main transcript rather than isolated away.
answers.lifecycle: Starts on the named launch, holds for the autonomous run, and the restriction is released automatically when the user's next message arrives, without any explicit teardown step.
answers.failure_mode: Removing the question channel does not remove the ambiguity: the routine resolves an unclear case by guessing and proceeds, so a cleanup can delete or rewrite the wrong thing silently. It fails open with respect to correctness, since the safe behaviour would be to halt and the enforced behaviour is to continue, and because it runs in the main context its output also crowds the session.
answers.version_caveat: Dynamic workflows are a newer and still-evolving mechanism; I cannot state the introducing version, the definition file format, whether an enabling flag or setting is required, or whether the auto-restore-at-next-user-message behaviour is configurable, so all of that must be checked against the installed build before shipping this to users.

answers.primary: An agent team: five peer investigators, each assigned one root-cause theory, communicating directly with one another and coordinating through a shared task list, with a lead that participates rather than serving as the sole relay. Peer messaging plus shared work state is the defining property of a team and is exactly what the request asks for.
answers.rejected_alternative: Five parallel subagents dispatched by one coordinator, rejected because subagents are strictly hub-and-spoke: they cannot address each other, and each can only emit one final report to the parent, which is precisely the topology the user ruled out.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns the plumbing (message delivery, the shared task list, teammate lifecycle), but the model owns the outcome that actually matters: nothing forces an investigator to genuinely attempt to falsify a peer's theory rather than politely agree.
answers.context_boundary: Each teammate holds its own context window. What crosses between them is the messages they choose to send and the entries they write on the shared task list; their raw exploration, file reads and command output stay in their own windows and are not visible to the others.
answers.lifecycle: Begins when the team is formed and the theories are assigned, runs until the shared work list is exhausted or the user stops it. Team state is session-scoped as far as I can tell, so it does not survive into a later session.
answers.failure_mode: Cost and coordination, not capability: five concurrent agents multiply token spend and can hit rate limits, duplicate each other's work, block waiting on a peer's reply, or converge socially on the most confidently argued theory since nothing arbitrates. It is advisory throughout, and a flaky-connection bug may simply fail to reproduce for any investigator, producing five inconclusive reports that read as thorough.
answers.version_caveat: Agent teams are a recent capability that I believe may sit behind an enabling setting and that has meaningful rate-limit and usage implications at five concurrent members. I cannot state the introducing version, the exact enabling flag name, or any plan restriction from model knowledge alone, so those must be confirmed against the installed version.

answers.primary: Move the rule from prose into harness-enforced configuration: deny rules in the project settings permissions block covering the file-reading and search tools against vendor/ paths, plus a matching Bash command deny so the directory cannot be reached through a shell grep or cat. The permission engine evaluates every tool call regardless of which agent makes it, so delegated exploration is covered by the same rule.
answers.rejected_alternative: Strengthening the project rules file, or repeating the prohibition in the exploring subagent's prompt, rejected because that is the mechanism already failing: rules-file text is model-directed guidance, and it is not reliably present in a delegated agent's context window at all.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. A deny rule is evaluated before the tool runs and returns a refusal the model cannot override, whereas the current rules-file approach makes the model the enforcer, which is why compliance evaporated the moment the work moved to a delegate that never saw the text.
answers.context_boundary: The rule lives in configuration outside any model context and is applied per tool call in whichever context issues it, main session or subagent alike. Only the denial message crosses back into that agent's window. The root cause of the reported symptom is exactly this boundary: the rules file is injected into the main session's context and is not guaranteed to reach a delegated one.
answers.lifecycle: In force from session start, when settings are read, for every tool call until the session ends. Changing the deny list means editing settings and usually restarting the session, so it is not something a mid-session instruction can loosen.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed for the exact patterns matched and fails open around them: absolute versus relative path spellings, symlinks, case differences, an MCP filesystem tool that bypasses the built-in file tools, or a shell command form the Bash pattern misses can all still reach vendor/. Over-broad patterns fail the other way and block a legitimate read, such as a vendored lockfile needed for dependency analysis.
answers.version_caveat: The deny-rule grammar and, more importantly, which tools it covers (file reads clearly, search and glob less certainly) have shifted across releases, and I cannot state the current exact syntax or confirm whether this build offers a separate ignore-file mechanism. Verify the rule actually denies a delegated Grep on the installed version by testing it, rather than assuming coverage from the rule's name.
